subject: Inputs, boilerplate, NULL and reactive relationships

messages.author: c8fe4075ec631c03
messages.subject: Inputs, boilerplate, NULL and reactive relationships
parts:
I've been playing with shiny over the weekend to see how it works, and I think its great.  My first application was in just about 60 lines and turned frozen data into interactive wonderment!

However, now I have more complex relationships between inputs and outputs (multiple inputs feed multiple outputs) I am becoming less clear about the construction of reactive inputs.

Simple question: If I refer to input$xyz in a reactive function such as a reactive plot, does the plot get generated:

1) any time the input xyz is updated AND is different
2) any time the input xyz is updated (different or not)
3) any time any input is updated

I have started writing logic like this:

xyz <- reactive(function() { input$xyz }

for each input, so as to make xyz a reactive dependency of the output function:

output$myPlot <- reactivePlot(function() {
  plot(xyz())
}

and hopefully is only re-drawn when input is updated and is different than before.

but this seems like wasted boilerplate to me.

-----

I've also been wiring code into all my reactive functions like so:

output$myPlot <- reactivePlot(function() {
  myxyz = xyz()
  if (is.null(myxyz) return NULL
  plot(myxyz)
}

To avoid plotting data when data is not available.  This seems to happen during start-up, especially when reactiveUI takes a few round trips to produce all the required input results.

This seems a pain to me; is there a better way?

----

I've looked through the source code briefly and haven't yet understood how the reactive graph is constructed - how does Shiny decide that myPlot() depends upon xyz() (And indeed (xyz()) upon input$xyz?

messages.subject: Re: Inputs, boilerplate, NULL and reactive relationships

1) any time the input xyz is updated AND is different
2) any time the input xyz is updated (different or not)
3) any time any input is updated

I have started writing logic like this:

xyz <- reactive(function() { input$xyz }

for each input, so as to make xyz a reactive dependency of the output function:

output$myPlot <- reactivePlot(function() {
  plot(xyz())
}

and hopefully is only re-drawn when input is updated and is different than before.

but this seems like wasted boilerplate to me.
Yes, if the ONLY thing you're doing in xyz is returning input$xyz then there shouldn't be a reason to do this at all.

I've also been wiring code into all my reactive functions like so:

output$myPlot <- reactivePlot(function() {
  myxyz = xyz()
  if (is.null(myxyz) return NULL
  plot(myxyz)
}

To avoid plotting data when data is not available.  This seems to happen during start-up, especially when reactiveUI takes a few round trips to produce all the required input results.

This seems a pain to me; is there a better way?

Not really a better way right now. It shouldn't be necessary *except* when reactiveUI enters the picture.

I guess it might make sense to introduce a special kind of error that means "this reactive function should return null" and a function that throws it if its input is NULL, so you could at least reduce the boilerplate to:

output$myPlot <- reactivePlot(function() {
  plot(essential(xyz()))
}

(I would've preferred "require" but that's taken by base; if anyone can think of a better name...)

I've looked through the source code briefly and haven't yet understood how the reactive graph is constructed - how does Shiny decide that myPlot() depends upon xyz() (And indeed (xyz()) upon input$xyz?

Here's the best explanation I've found; it's for Meteor, a JavaScript web framework from which Shiny's reactivity implementation draws inspiration:
http://stackoverflow.com/a/10293760/139922

Hopefully after reading that, you will be able to make sense out of react.R and then reactives.R.
